channel.title: The Beholder's Gazette
channel.description: Your premier source for satirical news from across the realms. All the news that's fit to print (or burn).

item.title: Fish Oil Pills Fail 2-Year Memory Trial; Sages Shrug
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: A two-year trial of 365 elders found fish oil reached the brain but did nothing for memory. Brother Wendell prescribes soup, not shiny jars.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, a two-year trial from the Kreck Infirmary has found that fish oil pills do nothing for memory. Three hundred and sixty-five elders, aged 55 to 80, swallowed a big daily dose of the brain-fat everyone calls DHA, or else a dummy capsule. At the end, the two groups remembered things equally badly.

The oil did get into the head. The scholars measured the fluid around the brain, and it rose about 17 percent after six months, so the stuff arrived. It just didn't do anything once it got there. The memory-keeping part of the brain shrank at the same rate in both groups, and nearly half the volunteers carried the family curse that makes the fading-mind sickness likelier. The study's lead sage said the results do not support these pills as a way to prevent it.

Now, the old herbals have always said to eat a little oily fish with your barley, and the new study nudges the same way. The sages suspect the goodness lives in the whole plate, the greens and beans and olive oil and fish eaten together, not in one golden bead. A fish does not become a wizard because you pressed it into a capsule.

I mention this because the aisle of supplement shops in the Lower City is a sad sight, friends. Jars of amber pearls, priced like a minor enchantment, promising to sharpen your wits, and every one of them smelling faintly of a harbor at low tide. Millions of you buy them. I am not scolding the buyers. I am scolding the people who put a picture of a clever owl on the label. If you want to see what happens when a shiny vial skips the proper testing, read my column on the bodega vial that turned out to be lip balm.

The Potion & Provisions Authority does not review these pearls the way it reviews healing draughts, which is why the labels can say "supports" and "promotes" and "may help" until the cows come home. The cows, I should add, are not buying them. The cows are fine.

So here is what I'd do with the gold you save. Walk every day. Sleep like a bear in a hollow log. Keep your friends close and your puzzles hard. Eat sardines on toast if you like sardines, and if you don't, don't force it. My friend Nyx tells me there's an app that trains your memory in six minutes a day. Go outside, Nyx. You'll remember it better.

This week's soup is a white bean and kale stew with a good glug of olive oil and a tin of sardines stirred in at the last minute, for those who dare. Three coppers a bowl, no label required.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: OpenEye Nears 30B gp Funding Round at 1.25T Valuation
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: OpenEye is closing a 30B gp funding round at a 1.25T gp valuation, led by desert sultans. Sterling calls the trimmed price a bold, scalable discount.
item.content:encoded:
OpenEye, makers of the ChattyGolem, is close to finishing a funding round of up to 30 billion gp at a valuation of 1.25 trillion gp, according to reports from the counting-houses. The Dune Sultanates and Coatl Capital are said to be leading the round, with signatures hoped for by the end of next week.

Now, some skeptics note that OpenEye earlier showed backers a price of 1.4 trillion gp, so this is a cut of 150 billion. I call it a pivot toward accessibility. Guildmaster Sam Altarman is not lowering his ask. He is democratizing the entry point for sultans. That is thought-leading, and I will not be taking questions from anyone who has not read my scroll.

Let us look at the fundamentals. OpenEye is, by any measure, a company that has the full attention of the realm. Eight provinces are suing it, and a hidden listening crystal was recently found in its boardroom. Where lesser guilds see liability, I see engagement. You cannot buy that kind of attention. Well, the sultans can, evidently, and at 1.25 trillion gp it is a bargain.

Some will say the round is a bridge to an eventual public listing, and that the sultans are paying a premium for the privilege of being first in line. To them I say: yes, exactly, and that is called vision. When I met Guildmaster Jeff Bezoar at a gala last spring, he told me, 'Sterling, valuation is just a number that hasn't been rounded up yet.' I have had that sentence embroidered on my morning-routine sparring vest.

The Brakka Stonesweat crowd will whine that the ChattyGolem has yet to turn a profit, and that a funding round this size could pay for a small kingdom. They always confuse a burn rate with a bonfire of opportunity. Rightsizing my expectations? Never. I rightsize other people's.

So here is where I stand. When a hungry golem needs 30 billion gp, the only sensible response is to ask how many more it can eat. I do my forty minutes of sword drills at dawn, and I do them for companies like this one.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • A lower price tag is just a higher growth story with better manners.
  • If sultans are in your cap table, you are in the right desert.
  • Never apologize for a number. Revise it, then call it a pivot.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Baseball Siege Opens: 103-Win Brewmasters Host Stingmantas
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: The baseball championship opens tonight in Milkwaukee, where the Brewmasters want a first title and I want that shiny foam finger. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the seventh bell this evening, the baseball championship, the World Siege, allegedly opens in Milkwaukee, where the 103-win Brewmasters host the Stingmantas of Tampering Bay in Game 1. The Brewmasters have never won a title. Their last trip to the Siege was in 1982, which is long enough ago that the beer from that year is allegedly still being poured.

The Brewmasters earned home-field the hard way: a franchise-record 103 wins, the most in the League, then a clean sweep of the Lost Angels Dodge-Rogues in the pennant melee. The Dodge-Rogues allegedly never saw it coming. Neither did a man named Orrin Pell, who was selling pretzels outside the ballpark and was eating one at the time. 'Four games, four losses, and they all looked surprised,' said Pell. 'Even the mascot looked surprised, and he's a sausage.'

The Brewmasters' ace, Jakob Mystery-Rowski, allegedly posted a 1.80 earned-run average and 252 strikeouts this season. Wizards of the stat tablet say that is very good. I say that is a lot of people sitting down confused. The Stingmantas, meanwhile, allegedly beat the Cleaveland Sentinels four games to two, which Lower City sources describe as 'a lot of swimming for one pennant.'

Rested Brewmasters versus freshly soaked Stingmantas is the matchup, and the Brewmasters have had days off to sharpen their bats. Some are calling it a mismatch. I am calling it a mismatch, allegedly, because the Tower District bookmakers have the home side at roughly three to two, and those nobles have never been right about anything but their own wine.

Ooh, a coin. Somebody dropped a gold piece by the Fish Street gate. It was a copper. Still nice.

Anyway. The Siege is a best-of-seven, played in a 2-3-2 pattern, which means the Stingmantas get three games at home and the rest of us get three days of arguing about it. Remember the Pale Stockings, who lost 121 games and still nearly crashed this party? Nobody has asked the Brewmasters about that. I will, if the pigeons stop circling the press box.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Donwald Regrets Picking Three Justices After Mail Ballot Loss
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: High Lord Donwald says he regrets appointing three justices who ruled against his mail ballot plan 7-2, and questions whether seats should be for life.
item.content:encoded:
High Lord Donwald of the Golden Towers told a magazine this month that he regrets appointing three of the nine justices of the High Courts. Those three helped strike down his plan to restrict mail ballots, seven votes to two. The interview was taken on the 28th and printed on the 1st, and it is the first time I can recall a High Lord reviewing his own appointees the way a landlord reviews a tenant.

For the record: the Court rejected the mail ballot restrictions on the 14th of last month. Only High Justice Clarion Thomme and High Justice Sam Alithor the Seated dissented. The other seven found the plan unlawful, and they include High Justices Gorsage, Kavanaw and Barrowgate, all three chosen by Donwald himself. The same bench had already struck down his sweeping tariffs and his order on birthright citizenship. Donwald put the resulting refund bill at roughly 400 billion gp, which he blames on the ruling rather than on the tariffs.

He called the decisions "very disappointing" and wondered aloud whether a seat held for life is wise when its occupant rules the wrong way. He said he wants "good decisions." He also said he "likes loyalty." Aides later clarified that he does not seek loyalty.

The trouble is procedural. The High Justices do not serve at the High Lord's pleasure. They serve at nobody's pleasure, and that is the entire design. A nomination is a one-time purchase with no returns desk. Donwald knows this well enough: he is currently asking the same Court to revive his grudge suit, which means he wants a favor from the bench in the same month he is grading it. The Court has not replied. It rarely replies promptly to anyone.

A courtier who asked not to be named, because they were not authorized to be awake, told me the High Lord's list of regrets "is longer than the list of justices, but the justices are on it first." Another pointed out that all three were recommended by the same advisory guild that now sends him sternly worded memoranda.

Promises Made this month: one, to seek a more loyal bench. Promises Kept: none. The Constitution of the Realm has no mechanism for it, and nobody has yet shown him the page.

Councilors of both parties declined to comment on the remarks, the only bipartisan act I have recorded this session. Off the record, the Blue Donkeys said the system is working. The Red Oliphants also said the system is working, and would not say which part. A motion expressing confidence in the Court carried without debate. I am not convinced anyone read it.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Foldable Phone Reviews Land: Duet Hides Crease, Weighs 254 g
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Critics say the 1,999 gp foldable phone hides its crease but runs hot and heavy. Nyx unboxed one on launch day and has feelings. Four eyes, with caveats.
item.content:encoded:
The reviews are in for the Pocketstone Duet, the 1,999 gp foldable phone from Discord Apple, and the verdict is: gorgeous, heavy, and please wait a year. Stores opened this morning, which means I have been standing in a queue since the third bell, and I regret nothing. (Well. My feet.)

Okay, the highlights! The 7.6-inch inner scrying pane uses a matte nano-texture that hides the crease in everyday use. You can still feel it with a fingertip and spot it at certain angles, but the hinge is, per one critic, "the smoothest action of any folding phone to date." The hidden camera under the glass! The full-day battery! Mana throughput that made my eyes water! I have not been this excited since the preorder scrolls went up.

Now the fine print. The Duet weighs 254 grams, five more than the previous flagship, which is a lot to ask of a wrist that also carries a spellbook. The outer pane is a cramped 5.4 inches. There is no telephoto lens, and the unlock rune is a thumb-glyph, not the face one. One reviewer called it "one of Discord Apple's messiest first-generation products in a long time." Another said he would wait for the second generation. A third noticed that it gets hot, and I can confirm this, because it is currently warming my lunch.

The apps are the real wrinkle. Many guild tools have not learned the new shape, so a messaging app sits in the middle of the big pane like a tiny scroll on a banquet table, surrounded by firmware glyph-shaped nothing. Discord Apple promises updated layouts, with a first batch arriving at launch. Launch-day stock is already gone, and new orders ship in February.

Byte, my pseudodragon, who now speaks only in ad copy, perched on the open device and said, "Unfold your potential." Then he slept on the hinge, which is the warmest spot in the Realms. I did not have the heart to close it.

Brother Tumbleberry will tell you to touch grass instead of paying 1,999 gp for a phone that opens like a book. I would point out that the Duet is a book you cannot read yet, because the apps are not ready. Still: four out of five beholder eyes. The crease is basically invisible, and I have looked very hard.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Damage Report: Gold spent: 1,999. Hinge pinches: 2. Lunches warmed: 1. Apps that fit the screen: pending.

item.title: Purple Worm Prophecy Typo Sends Brindlemoor Into Cellars
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: A purple worm prophecy carved above a Brindlemoor temple door had a typo. Half the town spent the night in cellars, including the Sleeping Mule's.
item.content:encoded:
THE SLEEPING MULE, CELLAR LEVEL 1 — A purple worm will not swallow Brindlemoor at the turning of the year, the Temple of the Lantern Hour confirmed this morning. The prophecy carved above its east door has been misread for eleven days, and about 400 residents slept underground on the strength of it.

The inscription, cut by a journeyman stonecutter and approved by the temple's augurs, reads: "A purple worm shall swallow Brindlemoor at the turning." The augurs now say the stonecutter dropped a line. The full verse reads: "A purple worm shall swallow Brindlemoor's tax rolls at the turning," a reference to a 200-year-old clerical dispute. The worm, they add, is a metaphor for the auditor.

I was in the cellar when the correction arrived. The Sleeping Mule held 61 residents, nine adventurers, one cheese wheel in a protective circle, and Keeper Bess Harrowgate, who had extended credit to everyone before they sat down. "A crowd is a crowd," Harrowgate said. "The ale does not care why they came." Her hit points were full. Her stock was not.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick, who signed the evacuation order at 2 a.m., said the town acted properly on the information it had. "We are aware of the typo," she said. "We are aware of the worm. The two are unrelated." She asked the temple to recut the stone and to put the full verse on a sign at street level, where a person might read the second half.

Chapter 9 moved quickly to claim the day. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick said the guild's delve permits remained valid throughout, and that the Undermaw had been "on track" for a worm-free season. When asked whether Chapter 9 sold maps to the cellars during the night, he said the maps were "informational." Receipts show 43 sold. I rolled poorly on getting a refund.

The Fourth Attempt's party bard, who asked to be named, said he had composed a 14-verse lament for the town by dawn and would now have to rewrite the ending. The party's fighter was at 12 hit points, mostly from sleeping on a barrel tap. The wizard cast augury on the stone at breakfast and got a result of "woe." The temple says the spell was cast on the wrong stone. Ten-foot poles lost this season: seven, one of them to a cellar door that was only a cellar door.

The stonecutter has not been charged, and said through the temple that he never claimed to be a prophet, only a man who is paid by the letter. Temple augurs will ask a real commune whether the purple worm itself is coming anyway. Answers are expected "around the turning," which is the kind of date I have always hated.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Damara Ships 40,000 Tons of Diesel to Waterdeep
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: The first diesel tanker from Damara sails for Waterdeep under Donwald's sanctions waiver. The cargo covers under two hours of the realm's thirst.
item.content:encoded:
A tanker carrying 40,000 tons of diesel left Damara on Thursday, bound for Waterdeep. It is the first shipment under the deal that lifted Czar Vlad's export ban, and the first time in years that sanctions-listed fuel has sailed toward the High Council's own harbors with a smile on it.

Vice-Chancellor Alexandr Novokov announced the sailing. He did not name the departure port. He did not name the landing port either. A good quartermaster keeps those secrets. A press office keeps them because nobody asked the right clerk.

I did the arithmetic. Waterdeep burns through that much diesel in under two hours. One ship, two hours. The war on the eastern front has lasted years. The fuel will last until lunch.

High Lord Donwald of the Golden Towers promised the stream would grow: 300,000 tons first, 500,000 in November, a million tons "immediately thereafter." Immediately, in Donwald's calendar, is a flexible unit. Vaasan scouts say the voyage takes up to three weeks. By then the first ship's cargo will be a rounding error and the second will be a rumor.

The High Council is furious. The Senate Chamber has already howled over the sanctions waiver and found it has no lever to pull. Councilors may write letters. Letters do not stop tankers. Tankers stop when they run out of sea.

Tension on the eastern front holds at about thirty-five siege-days, which is low, because everyone involved is now technically in business together. Czar Vlad sells fuel to the realm that sanctioned him. Donwald buys fuel from the ruler he calls a hard bargainer. Duke Volodar of Vaasa, whose soldiers are still being shelled by the same barrels' worth of refinery output, was not asked to the table. He was informed by letter.

The handshake, when it comes, will be firm. Two seconds. No hidden dagger detected. The dagger is in the contract, where it has always been, in small print, beneath the oil.

A word to the generals who say this eases prices at the pump. Maybe. A ration of field biscuit eases hunger too, for the length of one meal. I like biscuit. I do not mistake it for a harvest.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Strike Vote Passes 97.3% at Stellantern Wagonworks
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: Wagon builders gave their guild a 97.3% strike vote over job security and a plant the bosses want to sell. Nobody has walked out yet.
item.content:encoded:
They voted. Ninety-seven point three percent said yes to a strike vote at the auto plant.

More than 9,000 wagon builders at Stellantern Carriageworks in the Silver Marches cast ballots this weekend, and the strike vote came back nearly unanimous. The Unity Forge Guild, which speaks for them, now holds the power to call a walkout if talks stay stuck. They have not called one. The guild says a strike is a last resort and that a deal is still possible.

The sticking point is job security and the fate of the Brampstead plant in Ontarrow. Stellantern wants to sell it. First it plans to move the Jeap Compass wagon south to Waterdeep. Then it sells the empty building to a maker of armored war-carts. The company calls this 'footprint optimization.' That means they are leaving.

'I've bolted axles on that line for twenty-two years,' said Ingrid Coppergrip, a chassis-bolter at the Windersor Wagonworks, one of 6,400 voting there. 'They say sell the plant, not close it. Ask the people inside whether that's a difference.'

Here is how the strike gets legal. Under Marches law, either side must first ask for a 'no board' report. That is a scroll saying the arbitrators have given up on both of you. Nobody has filed one yet. So for now the vote is a sharpened axe leaning against the door. It is not a swing.

Meanwhile the Windersor line sits dark for another three-week shutdown, which the company calls a 'production adjustment.' Workers call it three weeks without pay. Coppergrip said the break is not a holiday: 'My rent doesn't shut down.'

The guild says it 'will not back down and accept a deal that weakens' the company's footprint in the Marches. Good. A weaker footprint is just a longer walk to the unemployment queue. For how the big wagon guild across the border handled its own vote of confidence, see our earlier report.

A guildmaster somewhere is surely drafting a statement about 'constructive dialogue.' That means he hopes you will stop asking about the plant. Do not stop asking about the plant.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Cryptocurrency Falls 2% to 82,423 gp as Lamp Oil Soars
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: Cryptocurrency slid 2% to about 82,423 gp as lamp oil stayed dear and traders braced for the Reserve's meeting. Barnaby checks the sums again.
item.content:encoded:
The price of Bitgold, the realm's best-known cryptocurrency, fell 2% in a day to roughly 82,423 gp, and is down 3% on the week. Traders blame expensive lamp oil: the Oil Lords of Amn have kept prices high, and high oil means the Federal Reserve of Waterdeep may raise rates again at its meeting on the 27th and 28th. (I have checked those dates four times.)

Let me put this on the Loaf Index, at four gold pieces a loaf. One Bitgold now costs about 20,606 loaves. Last autumn it peaked at 126,080 gp, or 31,520 loaves, before a single bad week of tariff threats wiped out some 19 billion gp in leveraged bets. That is 4.75 billion loaves, which is more bread than the realm has ever baked. It vanished because people borrowed money to bet on a magic coin. I do not wish to say I told you so. I wrote it down in my ledger, which is the same thing.

Here is the economics underneath. Rate hikes make borrowing dearer and make safe things, like a plain bond or a savings vault, pay more. That pulls gold away from coins that pay nothing at all. Oil feeds in because dear lamp oil pushes up the price of everything carried by cart, so the Reserve may feel it must hike. The Oil Lords' barrel price eased from near 110 gp to about 103 gp this month, which sounds like relief. It is not much relief. The markets still give about an 18% chance of a hike at any given meeting. (Eighteen percent is roughly one chance in five and a half. I have worked it out on three separate abacuses.)

Optimists are everywhere. One camp says Bitgold has climbed back above its 365-day moving average, a line that has come before past rallies, and that October has been kind to magic coins in eight of the last ten years. Sterling Vanmoor, naturally, is calling the dip a gift. I will only note that eight of ten is not ten of ten, and that the other two Octobers are the ones people remember. Anyone who says the market will sort itself out is welcome to explain it to the 19 billion gp.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, has not moved a single coin in three years. The boot is flat, dry and has never once been liquidated. She has asked me to report that her boot is up 0% this month, which beats the coin and also beats my nerves.

What this means for your pantry: If you hold Bitgold, do not borrow against it before the 28th. If you do not hold Bitgold, do not start now because a clerk called the bottom. Buy flour.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Weight-Loss Drug Test: Bodega Vial Was Lip-Balm Filler
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: The Cauldron had black-market weight loss drug vials tested. One held lip-balm filler and 13 bacterial colonies. Friends, boil a soup instead.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, the Cauldron Broadcasting Society has bought a few vials of an experimental weight-loss drug off the black market and sent them to a collegium for testing. The results, in the reporter's own word, were "terrifying." The drug is Rett-a-Tonic, which Eli Lilt Apothecaries is still testing as a next-generation slimming draught. It is nowhere near approved, and it is already for sale on the corner.

Our reporter ordered two vials from the internet. An online clinic promised a "health evaluation" at checkout, then mailed the stuff a week later without a single cleric ever speaking to him. A gym in Floridia took two days and a form that was supposedly read by a physician. Nobody read it. A third vial came from a bodega in the Cobblewick district for 90 gp, labeled "research use only, not for human consumption." Friends, that label is the most honest thing in the whole transaction.

The old herbals say never to drink from a bottle you can't name. The new study, from the Alchemy Collegium of Hawkeye Heights, agrees. The two online vials matched a basic reference sample, though the reference isn't the same stuff used in Eli Lilt's own trials, so even the good news comes with an asterisk. The bodega vial held no peptide at all. It held a filler used in perfumes and lip balms, plus 13 colonies of bacteria. A scholar at the collegium warned that anyone who injected it was inviting an infection.

A physician at a venerable collegium called the ease of buying these vials "astounding" and said the buyers are acting as guinea pigs. I'd say guinea pigs get better care. Eli Lilt noted that black-market vials lack the consistency of a regulated alchemist's work, and that one test can't prove any vial safe. It also pointed to reported deaths and injuries from illicit batches. According to Eli Lilt, the Potion & Provisions Authority and the Crown's magistrates have not yet moved against the sellers. The online clinic, the gym, and the vial company didn't answer the Cauldron's questions.

I know it's hard, friends. A weight-loss drug costs a fortune when it's real, and the sellers know exactly who is desperate. But please don't inject mystery lip balm into your thigh. If you want to feel lighter, the old herbals recommend a walk, a good night's sleep, and a bowl of something warm and full of vegetables. My friend Nyx Spindlecoil says there's a scrying app that can check a vial's purity from across the room. Go outside, Nyx, and take the vial with you. Then pour it out.

This week I recommend white bean and kale soup, three coppers a pot, and it has never once contained a bacterial colony I didn't put there on purpose.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Earnings Beat, Capex Cut: Teslarc Slips 3% Anyway
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Teslarc beat earnings forecasts and trimmed its capex plan to 20B gp, yet shares slid after hours. Sterling calls it a bold pivot in how to win.
item.content:encoded:
Teslarc Carriages beat Wall Street's quarterly earnings forecast on Wednesday, then watched its shares slide about 3 percent after the closing bell. Adjusted earnings came to 48 copper pieces a share against the 43 the Merchant Princes expected, and the guild trimmed its capital spending plan for the year to roughly 20 billion gp. Some people see a stock falling after good news. I see investors who simply have not been briefed on the vision.

Let me walk you through the winning numbers. Revenue landed at 28.05 billion gp, comfortably ahead of the 27.9 billion gp forecast, and flat on last year, which in my book is called stability at scale. Free cash flow came in at 1.53 billion gp, down 62 percent. I prefer to say it was reallocated into the future. Carriage sales fell 3 percent and the energy-crystal wing fell 16 percent, but the services wing grew 33 percent, because nothing says growth like billing people after they have already bought the thing.

Now the skeptics, and you know which dwarf I mean, will say that cutting the capital budget from over 25 billion gp to 20 billion gp while operating costs climb is just moving the bill from one pocket to another. Wrong. That is called capital efficiency. The money still goes to the self-driving Model Why coaches, the Spectercab and the walking servant golems. It simply goes there under a different line item, which is the most elegant pivot a guild can make.

It also lands one day after Guildmaster Elon Muskrat told SpellX investors on their call that merging his two guilds would be a 'good idea,' and that special committees of both boards are already talking. A merger! I get goosebumps. I met Guildmaster Elon once at a charity joust, and he told me, 'Sterling, a company is just a spreadsheet with a dream.' I framed that. Frankly, the only thing better than one guild with a dream is two guilds sharing the same dream and the same bill.

So the shares dipped. Dips are discounts for visionaries. Every great adventurer buys the dip, then explains to his party why the dip was always part of the plan.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Beat the forecast, then pivot the story before the market can.
  • Cut spending in one column and raise it in another. Nobody audits both.
  • When profits wobble, announce a merger.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: E-Bike Jousting Draws Hundreds in Londrake Park
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: Two armored men jousted on rental e-bikes before hundreds in a Londrake park. Limewyrm says its mounts are 'not for jousting.' Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell past noon on Sunday, two men in full plate armor allegedly charged at each other on rented e-bikes in a Londrake park, lances lowered, while hundreds of spectators watched. The e-bike jousting was filmed, the footage spread across every scrying pool in Cormyr, and by Wednesday Limewyrm Rentals had issued a statement that its mounts are "not for jousting."

The riders, allegedly, were a half-elf named Pell Rushwick, who calls himself a "performance artist," and an actor billed as Sir Bartleby the Loud. Both wore armor. Both rode the bright green Limewyrm bikes that clutter every Londrake pavement. Nobody has confirmed whether the lances were also rented, but a lance does look like it was made for this.

"I came for a picnic," said Odo Pennyfeather, a baker who was holding a cheese wheel at the time. "Then a man in a breastplate went past me at the speed of a trotting pony, making a sound like a kettle. I dropped the cheese. Best afternoon of my year."

Limewyrm's spokesperson said the company "appreciates the medieval spirit" but that safety comes first, that the bikes are built for city transport, and that nobody should recreate the stunt. The Lower City desk notes that this is exactly what a company says about a thing that is going to be recreated.

Ooh. There was a coin in the grass near the jousting lane, a real shiny one, with a little dragon on it. Anyway. I put it in my pocket, allegedly, as evidence.

Rushwick has announced a second jousting tourney for the thirty-first of the month, location to be determined. Londrake's Park Wardens have allegedly not yet commented. Neither have the pigeons, and I will say no more about the pigeons, who were definitely there and definitely smug.

Scholars of the lists point out that the Tower District nobles have jousted on far worse for centuries and billed the Crown for the horses. Rival desk-man Hollis Delvewright may wish to explain why that is acceptable and a rented bicycle is not.

For now, the city's guilds advise that e-bikes are meant for getting to the tavern, not for knocking a man off one. Allegedly, a few bikes were returned dented. The deposit was allegedly kept.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Ohyo Vale Governor Race: Attack Ads Fact-Checked, Both Fail
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A fact-check of the governor's race attack ads in Ohyo Vale finds both campaigns technically right and practically misleading. The Chamber is unsurprised.
item.content:encoded:
A fact-check of the attack ads in the Ohyo Vale governor's race has found that both campaigns told the truth in the way a man tells the truth when he is standing on your foot. The two candidates, the gentleman from the biotech guilds and the lady from the Healers' College, each paid for thirty seconds of selective quotation, and each is now owed a correction nobody will air.

The gentleman is Vivrek Ramaswizard. His allied super guild ran an ad stating that the lady, Healer Amity Actune, was rated "insufficient" in medical knowledge. This is accurate. The rating came from a single evaluator during her internship in 1994. Later reviews called her knowledge "excellent." The ad also says she missed a Disease Council training after tripping on a dog gate. She did, in an old podcast, and it was not medical training, and it was months before the plague. The ad further says police found her drinking while on prescription drugs. The drug was for a migraine, and the police report notes she was not intoxicated. I have read the report. It is shorter than the ad.

Then there is the line crediting Actune with praising the socialist Mayor Zohrad Mamdwarni. The cited source does not mention her. Mamdwarni's name appears in the script only next to clips of High Lord Donwald praising him, which the ad leaves for the viewer to enjoy as a gift.

In fairness to the Chamber's rules of balance, the Actune camp was no better. Its ad calls Ramaswizard's old firm, Axovault Biomancers, a "dubious pharmaceutical company." That is an opinion, and opinions are protected. It says he pushed a drug he knew did not work. The drug was in trials, was unapproved, and could not legally be sold to anyone, so he was at most promoting a potion he hoped would work. It says his company charged sick children $3 million. The listed price is $2.7 million, before surgery and without insurance. Round numbers are the oldest tool in the chamber. A quoted line, "we are making money, that's what's most important," is a paraphrase of a conversation he denies.

Promises Made this session: nineteen. Promises Kept: the one about being "tough but fair," which both sides keep sending me in writing. As I noted when midterm ad spending topped ten billion gold pieces, a great deal of coin is being spent to say less than the facts already say.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me both ads "tested very well." Neither tested for accuracy. Early voting continues. The ads have aired. Nobody read the fact-check.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Envydia Drops Open AI Models for Local Agents
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Envydia's new open AI models run agents on your own rune-PC, no cloud needed. Nyx tested them for three days. The quests got done. The hearth did not.
item.content:encoded:
OKAY. Envydia has released a fresh batch of open AI models built to run agents, the little spellcasting helpers that book your errands and file your paperwork, and I have had them running on my workbench since Monday. This is the greatest thing to happen to my workbench, and I include the time Byte set it on fire.

The lineup is the Nemotome 3.5 family. The big one, Nemotome 3.5 Super Vellum, packs 120 billion parameters and is aimed at guilds that want agents handling document sorting, ledger work, and insurance-claim scrolls. Envydia says that once a guild post-trains it on its own records, it finishes tasks faster than Anthropyre's Clawde Opera-5 and the ChattyGolem-6 line from OpenEye, including Sunforged and Moonforged. That's a vendor claim, obviously. I verified it by being delighted.

The smaller Nemotome 3.5 Zap runs on 74 billion parameters and is built for home use. It lives on a rune-PC with the new Rune-Spark chip, so your agent can browse, reason through multistep chores, and call tools without sending a single thought to a distant cloud. Archmage Carrie Briskwick, Envydia's Warden of Open Grimoires, promises that adventurers can "delegate everyday projects" without the cloud ever seeing them. A baby model, Zap Tiny, arrives later this month. I have already cleared a shelf.

Now the review. The mana throughput is staggering. My agent booked a tavern table, renegotiated my familiar's subscription, and reorganized my spell components alphabetically in under four minutes. The runic latency is so low I never saw it blink. Then the firmware glyph on the Rune-Spark began to glow, the hearth room reached the temperature of a forge, and the agent, working locally and therefore privately, ordered nine hundred gold pieces of copper wire to "improve airflow." No cloud saw this. Nobody can refund it.

Byte, who now speaks only in ad copy, perched on the smoking rune-PC and announced, "Open weights. Open hearts. Open flames." The chip is also not cheap, and the open model is free only in the way a free dragon egg is free. Brother Tumbleberry will say I should touch grass. The grass, Brother, is on fire, and my agent is billing me for it.

Still, an open model I can retrain on my own data, running in my own cellar, with no monthly fee? Envydia, I will follow you into any flame. Five out of five beholder eyes.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Burns sustained: 2. Copper wire ordered: 900 gp. Eyebrows: pending.

item.title: Young Red Dragon Hoard Survey Finds Cheese Ripened in Hours
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: The Cellars Board's cheese survey found a young red dragon's hoard ripens cheddar in hours. Keeper Harrowgate is not saying no to the permit.
item.content:encoded:
TANNER'S ROW, CELLAR LEVEL 1 (ONE FLIGHT DOWN, SIX STEPS OF SOOT) — The Brindlemoor Public Cellars Board finished its cheese survey this morning and found that the hoard of the young red dragon Skorvath ripens cheddar in about four hours. The permit to extend that hoard under three cellars remains tabled.

Inspector Corwin Tallowby set out nine wheels of cheese at measured distances from the hoard's edge: one at forty feet, one at thirty, and so on down to a wheel placed, in his words, 'at a distance I would call rude.' He logged each hour by candle. The forty-foot wheel was unchanged. The thirty-foot wheel was sharp. The wheel at ten feet had, by midday, developed opinions.

'It is a legitimate finding,' Tallowby said, holding a clipboard singed along one edge. 'I cannot classify it. The Board has categories for spoiled, aged, and unverified. This is a fourth category, and I have had to invent a form.'

The Cellars Board ranks heat damage under cellar hazards, but the cheese was not damaged. By the inspector's tasting, it was excellent. He declined to say how excellent on the record. His clipboard says 'very.'

Skorvath attended in person, which is to say it lay across the cellar floor on top of 11,400 gold pieces and tried to look like a small dragon. 'I would like it noted that I did not ask for the cheese,' it told the Board. 'I filed for storage. The cheese is a gift of the property.' Its two earlier fires, it added, were 'a matter of record and of regret.'

Keeper Bess Harrowgate of the Sleeping Mule, whose cellar is one of the three in question, has stopped answering the permit question with a flat no. 'I'll say this,' she told me. 'I have cheese on my slate from a supplier who wants his money in three tendays. If it's ready in four hours, that supplier and I have a new conversation.' She would not say yes. She did stop using the word 'no.'

The Fourth Attempt's hirelings, who drink at the Mule, were less sure. The party's bard, who asked to be named, called the findings 'a hoard with a cheese problem and a cheese with a hoard problem.' Ansel Pottage, steward of the hirelings, asked only that the permit's fine print be read aloud 'all the way to the end, including the part about the floor getting warm.'

Reeve Fennick, asked by the Board for comment, said, 'We are aware of the cheese.' She then asked who was responsible for the smell, and was told the answer was 'delicious.'

Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society confirmed it has opened a file. A claims adjuster said the question is whether a dragon-ripened cheese counts as fire damage or a windfall. Neither category has a form either.

The Board will resume the permit hearing after a second survey, this one of mold. Ten-foot poles lost this season: seven. The seventh was used to measure the forty feet and was never recovered; I rolled poorly on where I set it down.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Embassy Accuses Silver Marches of Election Interference
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: Waterdeep's embassy says the Marches meddled in the November midterm election by opposing tariffs. The proof: a fact sheet and eleven names.
item.content:encoded:
The Waterdeep embassy in the Silver Marches issued a fact sheet on Wednesday accusing Marcher politicians of election interference ahead of the November 3 midterm vote. The stated offense: opposing tariffs. Loudly. In public.

I read the document twice. It names eleven individuals. It does not say what they did, or tie any of them to the Marcher crown. Eleven is also the number of people prosecuted for voting illegally in Waterdeep between 2012 and 2024, which suggests the clerks had a list and a deadline. Evidence: none detected. Siege-days since Donwald's ballot-counting pause on the Calimshan front: still counting.

The embassy's case rests on three planks. Royal Minister of Industry Melonie Jolly said in August that the Marches were "targeting products that will target states" in Waterdeep. In September she took meetings with Blue Donkey officials in Bastion and Chikraggo. Margrave Dug Fjord of Ontarrow, meanwhile, ran an anti-tariff ad campaign using clips of High Lord Ronan Raygun, who disliked tariffs. Donwald responded to that one last year by walking out of trade talks. The ad is a weapon. Raygun is the ammunition. He is dead and cannot be reached for comment.

Jolly rejected the charge. She says she was in Waterdeep to attract investment, and that the governors and presidential hopefuls she met are just "so many governors and potential presidential candidates." A tribunal would call that a confession. A merchant would call it Tuesday.

Envoy Pete Hookstra, the embassy's chief, was careful. Waterdeep is "monitoring it, evaluating it," he said, and "if some of it becomes election interference then America will respond." That is not an accusation. That is a hand resting on a hilt. Chancellor Mark Carnie of the Marches had already given his position: "We don't get ourselves involved in their elections, they don't get themselves involved in our elections." Firm. Brief. No hidden dagger detected.

Here is what I see from the wall. The Marches built a tariff dispute that Waterdeep started. Waterdeep now calls the Marches' response a campaign against its ballot box. The Red Oliphants face a rough midterm season and need an enemy with a border, and a polite neighbor with maple banners is the cheapest enemy in the realm. Honest enemies I respect. This is a press release in armor.

Tension between the two realms holds at roughly twelve siege-days, mostly paperwork. The Marches have not yet replied to the embassy. If they do, expect politeness, followed by more politeness, which is the Marcher way of loading a catapult.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Portmantle City Workers Vote 93% to Strike
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: Eight hundred Portmantle city workers voted 93% to authorize a strike over layoffs and pay, while managers keep their raises. Brakka did the sums.
item.content:encoded:
Eight hundred city workers in Portmantle just voted 93 percent to strike.

The Scribes' Union, which counts the city's number-wardens, signal-mages and picture-inkers, authorized the walkout this week. It could start as early as the first of Frostfall. That's the second city-worker strike vote in the western lowlands this month, after the library walkout in Corvallow.

Here's how we got here. Ten months of wage talks went nowhere. The Scribes' Union declared impasse on the 24th of Harvestmoon. A thirty-day cooling-off period began on the second of this month. The city's final offer is about 9.1 million gp in new spending. The union's counter costs about 19.8 million gp. Do the subtraction yourself. It isn't hard.

The Lord Mayor's labor office says it is "committed to a fair agreement that balances employee contributions with city finances and taxpayer responsibility." That means they want the workers to chip in and the managers to keep theirs.

"They want to cut our people while the managers collect raises and the top clerks walk out with six-figure exit purses," said Kari Kotch, president of the Scribes' Union. "Their own numbers don't add up. We checked. We're the ones who do the adding."

Last year's budget scroll proposed axing 274 posts. Managers were a fifth of the payroll but only an eighth of the cuts. Somebody up there is very good at protecting their own.

And there's a second wave coming. The Navvies' Lodge 483, about 750 bridge-menders, park-keepers and hall-sweepers, votes next week. Business manager Ryan Sotomajor expects eighty percent or better. These are the same navvies who struck for three days back in the Year of the Rain and shut down the city's first municipal strike in twenty years. Put both unions together and more than 1,500 workers could be on the line by year's end.

"I mend the Weir Street bridge," said Odrek Pitchhammer, a Lodge bridge-mender for twenty-two years. "Nobody notices till the bridge isn't there. Same goes for the folks who run the payroll ledgers. Try getting paid without them."

The city says it has a budget hole. Fine. Council members floated a Fair Share Levy on rich guilds that pay their top bosses a hundred times what they pay their sweepers. It would raise 72 million gp a year. Funny how nobody wants to talk about that one at the bargaining table.

Guildmasters will tell you a strike hurts everyone. It does. So does a hole in the budget with a manager's raise sitting at the bottom of it.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Jobless Claims Fall to 194,000; Guilds Hoard Hirelings
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: Weekly jobless claims fell to 194,000 as guilds neither hire nor fire. I have run the sums on this calm, and my pantry does not feel calm.
item.content:encoded:
The Ministry of Guild Labor reported on Thursday that weekly jobless claims fell to 194,000, below the 200,000 the counting-house wizards predicted. That is the lowest the figure has sat in roughly sixty years. (I have checked this four times, and the sixty years is real.) Continuing claims, meanwhile, rose by 25,000 to 1.728 million, which is the kind of detail that gets buried in paragraph six, so I put it in paragraph one.

Here is what the numbers say. Few hirelings are being dismissed, which is good. Few are being taken on either, which, as I explained after the 29,000-hireling month, is the other half of a "low-hire, low-fire" realm. Guilds are standing in a ring with their arms folded. A baker who is not sacked still cannot find a new bakery if the old one closes. Picture a very polite game of musical chairs where the music has stopped and nobody will remove a chair.

Now the Loaf Index. At a rough 4 copper per loaf, 194,000 claimants is a queue that would need 776,000 coppers a week to feed on bread alone. That is one fewer queue than last week, by 6,000 souls, or 24,000 coppers of bread I am not worrying about. I am worrying about it anyway. (Please do not tell Sterling Vanmoor; he will call it "a victory lap" and I will have to lie down.)

The reason this matters is the lamp-oil inflation I keep writing about. The Federal Reserve of Waterdeep, which the clerks call the Reserve, raised its rate by a quarter point last month to between 3.75% and 4.00%, and it meets again on the 27th and 28th. Everyone expects it to hold. A strong jobs picture is what lets the Reserve keep its hands in its pockets. A weak one would force it to choose between prices and payrolls, and with oil climbing because of the war in Calimshan, both are already sore.

So the news is mildly good and should be read mildly. A low claims number only means that nobody is being let go. It tells you nothing about whether your cousin, who was let go in spring, will ever be hired again. The rise in continuing claims suggests he will not be hired soon. Low-fire, low-hire markets feel fine to people who already have a stool and awful to people who are still standing.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, says the economy is "a pot that has stopped boiling and also stopped simmering." I told her that is not a technical term. She said the boot has not lost a coin since the Great Wheat Panic. I could not argue.

What this means for your pantry: keep your stool, keep a month of flour, and do not quit your guild to "find yourself" this winter.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Flu Season Arrives Two Months Early in the West
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: The flu season has started in September, with 140.6 cases per 100,000 folk and a western children's infirmary swamped. Get your flu shot, friends.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, the winter cough has come early. The flu season, which the clerics usually expect in the cold months, began climbing in early September, and the Clerics' Disease Council now says activity is rising across the realm. Nationally it is still low, but the western coast is already coughing.

The old herbals say the sick season follows the first frost. The new studies, as reported by a records firm that counts sniffles for a living, say otherwise: 140.6 visits for flu per 100,000 folk in the week of mid-September, the highest for that time of year in five years and double the last two autumns. One western children's infirmary saw 150 little patients in two weeks, where last year it saw ten. Its healer told reporters, "We're about two months early." I do not like the sound of that, friends.

The Disease Council's own tally for the week ending the third of October shows flu tests coming back positive 3.6 percent of the time, and 3,334 folk in hospital beds, mostly the elderly. Hospital visits have crept up since the end of summer. Several scholars guess a new strain of the H1N1 sort is dodging the defenses people built up from old coughs and old vials. Another reminded everyone that an early start says little about how long the season lasts or how hard it bites. Seasons often come in waves, so an early H1N1 wave may be followed by H3N2 or the B kind. Nobody is promising you a short winter.

Now the good part. The strain going around is close to the one in this year's vial, so the vials the Ministry has been fretting over in other matters are, for flu, a good match. Get your flu shot early. The scholars say before the middle of October if you can, which is now, so go on. Arm out, sleeve up, a boiled sweet afterward. The Potion & Provisions Authority has even approved a newer kind of shot for those aged fifty and over, though I note it will not be cheap, and cheap is where I put my trust.

Meanwhile, wash your hands, sleep at least eight hours, and keep your cough off the elderly. A halfling who skips sleep during a flu surge is asking for a visit from me and my ladle.

My friend Nyx tells me there is a tracker for flu now, with a live map and push alerts. Go outside, Nyx, preferably after your shot. For everyone else, this week's recommendation is a chicken-and-ginger broth with plenty of garlic, simmered two hours and sipped slowly under a blanket.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Automaker Earnings Hit 50B gp; 20B Buyback Follows
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: General Mounts posts 50B gp in quarterly earnings and approves a 20B gp stock buyback. Sterling Vanmoor calls a shrinking shareholder table a growth story.
item.content:encoded:
General Mounts, the carriage-maker of the Cleaveland-adjacent Iron Marches, reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday: 50 billion gp in revenue, 3.3 billion gp in profit, and a brand-new 20 billion gp stock buyback with no expiration date. I want you to sit with that last part, because most guilds can't even schedule a meeting with no expiration date.

Here is the pivot. Guildmaster Mary Barrow's scribes have been buying the company's own shares back for a year, and the guild now has 849 million shares in circulation, down from 904 million at the start of the year. General Mounts is, in the most literal sense, becoming more exclusive. Some call that shrinking. I call it scaling inward. It's the same energy as the Merchant Princes' latest earnings season, and I am here for it.

The skeptics, and you know who you are, Brakka, will point out that the guild also took 3.6 billion gp in what the report calls an "EV strategic realignment" this year. That is the accounting term for a stable of enchanted lightning-carriages nobody wanted to buy. I prefer another term: a bold early-stage experiment in discovering what the customer doesn't want. Very few guilds have the courage to lose 3.6 billion gp on purpose. Guildmaster Barrow simply labeled it, set it aside, and told the investors to look at the other number, the 4.1 billion gp that came in before the lightning-carriages were mentioned. That is thought leadership.

The dividend, meanwhile, holds at 18 copper pieces per share, payable in mid-December, which is a very generous way of saying "thanks for staying." The guild also nudged its full-year forecast: profit before the tax-collectors is now expected at 14.5 to 15.5 billion gp, a tighter range than before. Tighter is better. Ask any rightsized adventuring party.

When I met Guildmaster Jeff Bezoar at a gala last spring, I asked him about buybacks. He looked at me over his goblet and said, "Sterling, the best investment is the one you already own." I wrote it on my forearm. I have since bought back three of my own sword-routine scrolls, at a premium, from myself. The returns have been exceptional.

Will the 20 billion gp buyback make the stock go up? Almost certainly, because there will be fewer of them. Will it build a single new carriage? No, and that is precisely the point. Builders build. Visionaries retire shares.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • If your product line is struggling, buy your own stock until the problem becomes everyone else's.
  • A 3.6 billion gp loss is a "realignment" if you say it slowly.
  • Fewer shareholders means bigger slices. Ignore anyone who says the pie is the same size.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.
